title: An Amazing, Eye-Opening Following Directions Strategy
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents what he calls the "line strategy," a ten-step exercise designed to sharpen how well students follow directions. Teachers mark a line on the classroom floor, give simple one-step directions in a soft voice, and send any student who doesn't comply immediately to stand on the line, gradually layering in more directions while offering compliant students the chance to return to their seats. Framed as a listening game rather than a punishment, the exercise is meant to be experienced rather than explained in advance, so students draw the lesson - that they need to listen the first time - through direct consequence. He closes by suggesting the exercise reveals as much to teachers about their students' true capability as it teaches students about listening.
points: Mark a physical line on the classroom floor at least 20 feet long for the exercise.
Give simple, one-step directions in a soft tone, then send non-compliant students to stand on the line.
Offer students a chance to return to their seats as soon as they show they're listening.
Never explain the strategy beforehand - let students discover the lesson through direct experience.
Frame it as a listening game, Simon Says-style, never as a punishment or humiliation.
quotes: Does it seem as if an evil, invisible force is encrypting your voice, and the message your students are getting is actually an indecipherable warble?
When your students seem to be at their…ahem…least responsive, give a simple, one-step direction—only once and in a soft tone and volume of voice .
Without saying another word, notice who is and isn’t following your direction. Quickly approach those who aren’t, or who didn’t, and ask them to stand with both feet on the line.
It’s important that you don’t explain the line strategy to your students or why you’re doing it. Don’t add a lecture, an admonishment, or say more than you need to in order to conduct the exercise.

Deep down all students want to be part of what is right and true and desirable. And so when asked to stand on a line that represents the opposite of that, it burns a hole right through the bottoms of their shoes.
When you get a glimpse of what is possible, when you peer into what could be, it will cast your students in an unfamiliar light.
